title.narrative: Adaptation of agricultural value chains to climate change in Madagascar – PrAda 2+

description.narrative:
Following five consecutive years of severe drought, Madagascar is experiencing significant economic challenges, including a sharp decline in agricultural productivity—with annual crop losses estimated at USD 122 million—and rising food insecurity affecting approximately 69% of the population.
In response, this adaptation project aims to catalyze a systemic shift from climate-vulnerable subsistence farming to a market-oriented, sustainable, and climate-resilient agricultural economy in Madagascar. It prioritizes support for smallholder farmers and local actors across five key value chains—vanilla, cloves, coffee, pepper, and peanuts—by developing critical assets and promoting climate-resilient revenue generation through targeted technical assistance.
The project is structured around three interconnected and complementary components. First, the Technological Component aims to improve CRA production by introducing adapted crop varieties, delivering agrometeorological advisory services, and strengthening technical capacities for CRA implementation. Second, the Financial Component supports CRA investment by providing non-repayable grants to smallholders through FDA’s public on-granting mechanism, enhancing technical support for financial institutions, and upgrading community-level financial systems such as mobile banking. Third, the Market Component promotes an enabling environment for CRA adoption by building entrepreneurial capacities and reinforcing institutional frameworks for smallholder farmers, cooperatives, and value chain actors engaged in input supply, production and post-harvest processes.
The project is implemented by GIZ, acting as both Accredited Entity (AE) and Executing Entity (EE), alongside the Agricultural Development Fund (FDA)—a key public financing entity under the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock. Notably, FDA has a proven track record of implementing projects with the World Bank, ADB, EU, and AFD, and of complying with their respective financial requirements.
The financing structure includes a EUR 43.6 million grant from GCF, complemented by EUR 17.7 million in co-financing from the German government (BMZ), bringing the total project envelope to EUR 61.3 million. This configuration is expected to directly benefit approximately 314,800 and indirectly reach an additional 2.6 million people—together accounting for nearly 10% of Madagascar’s population.
